text: Hi, how's it going? I'm a big coffee lover, so I guess I'll start there. I can't really start my day without a cup of coffee, and this morning was no different. I had one before I came to take this test, and I'm already looking forward to another one once it's over. I work in IT, and my days are pretty busy. I live in an apartment, and I'm pretty much a homebody. In my free time, I like listening to music, playing computer games, and reading. So, yeah, that's me in a nutshell: coffee, music, and my computer. I'm happy to be here, and I hope I do well today!

Well, to be honest, most young people here dream of working for a big name, like Naver, Kakao, or a major electronics company. The number one reason is job security. Getting hired at a big company is like hitting the jackpot in Korea. The pay is great, the benefits are good, and your parents get to brag about you at family gatherings! I mean, a young coworker of mine said the same thing the other day. Another reason is the tech companies feel cool and modern. You can wear hoodies to work, bring your own laptop, and work on stuff millions of people use. But the thing is, the competition is crazy. Some people study for years just to get one interview. I think that's why so many young people feel stressed out. Anyway, I get it. Everyone wants a stable and fun job.

One industry that's really taking off right now is K-content: dramas, movies, and K-pop. Ten years ago, nobody outside Asia knew about it. Now my friends in other countries are watching Korean dramas! I think it's growing so fast because of the internet. You know, streaming services like Netflix made it easy for anyone in the world to watch our shows. Another reason is that Korean companies spend a lot of time training their artists. Take my favorite K-pop group. They practice for years before they debut. The stories are also pretty fresh, so people don't get bored. To make a long story short, it worked because of good quality and good timing. I'm honestly proud of it.

Honestly, I didn't get here overnight. When I first got into IT, I knew almost nothing about servers. So I studied at night after work for a network certification. I failed the first time! I was so bummed out, but I wasn't going to give up. I tried again, and I finally passed. Besides that, I also worked on my English, because our company works with foreign vendors. I'd listen to English podcasts on my way to work every day. Another big thing was learning from my seniors. I'd stay late and watch them fix problems, and I learned so much that way. Looking back, those late nights really paid off. The key is just to keep learning, even when it's tough.

I'm kind of into K-pop, which might surprise people because I'm not that young anymore! I even have a favorite group. I listen to their songs almost every night when I play computer games. I mean, their music just gets me pumped up. But when I want to chill, I put on some slow ballads. My favorite singer for that is a famous ballad singer. Her voice is so calm and warm, and her lyrics hit me right in the heart. Oh, and I listen to music while I work, too, usually something soft with no lyrics, so it doesn't distract me. Honestly, I can't live without music. It's like coffee for my ears.

Well, it all started at home. There was always music playing, and we had a pile of cassette tapes. The radio was on every night. I couldn't help but pick it up. Back then, I liked Korean ballads and some pop songs that my family loved. Then in high school, I got into rock and played the same CD a hundred times! These days, my taste has changed. I listen to K-pop and a lot of calm music. I guess I just get tired easily now, so I like softer sounds. But the funny thing is, I still sing those old songs in the shower. Some things never change.

Yes! The most memorable one was a K-pop concert in Seoul a couple of years ago. My friend got us tickets as a surprise for my birthday. I almost didn't believe her, because those tickets sell out in seconds! We got there early, and the place was packed. I was probably the oldest guy in the crowd, holding a light stick like a total newbie. When the lights went down, the whole place went crazy. I couldn't help but scream. My friend couldn't stop laughing at me. At the end, everyone sang the last song together, and I got goosebumps. It was a total blast. I still listen to that playlist and think of that night.

Well, we have all kinds of hotels in Korea. In big cities like Seoul and Busan, most hotels are right downtown, close to the subway or a busy shopping area. That's really handy for business trips, like when I go up to Seoul for meetings. Then there are resort hotels near the beach or the mountains. Those are huge, with pools and fancy restaurants. If you go to Jeju, you'll see hotels right by the ocean. One thing I love is the breakfast buffet. Honestly, I choose hotels based on the food! And the service is great. The staff is polite, and the rooms are always clean. I'd say Korean hotels are pretty hard to beat.

The hotel I'll never forget was a resort hotel in Jeju. I don't remember the exact name, but it was right by the ocean. We went there with my family on summer vacation. The place was beautiful, with a big pool and a garden full of palm trees. But on the second night, a typhoon hit the island! The wind was howling, and then, boom, the power went out. It was pitch dark, and everybody started to freak out. So we all sat on the floor with our phone lights on and told silly stories. Someone did a funny voice, and everybody cracked up. The next morning, the staff handed out free coffee. It was a total mess, but I remember it as a really cozy night.

The last time I stayed in a hotel was about a month ago. It was in Seoul, for a business trip. I had a big meeting the next morning, so I took the train up the day before. I checked in around 7, and my room was on the 15th floor with a nice city view. I dropped my bag and headed to dinner with a coworker. When I got back, I opened my bag and realized I'd left my phone charger at home! My phone was at 5 percent. I called the front desk, and they said, "No problem, sir." They brought one up in five minutes. Wow, that was service. After that, I read a book and had a hot shower. In the morning, I had two cups of coffee at the buffet and checked out. Lesson learned: always pack the charger!

Hello, I just moved into the building, and I have a few questions about recycling. First, where do I put the recycling?. Okay. And what days do you pick it up?. Got it. Do I need to wash the plastic bottles and cans first?. Also, what about food waste? Is there a special bin or a special bag?. Oh, and one last thing: how do I throw away big stuff, like an old chair? Do I need to pay for that?. Perfect. That really helps. Thanks so much for your time!

Hi, it's your neighbor from next door. Welcome to the building! I hope you're settling in okay. I wanted to talk to you about something small, so please don't take this the wrong way. Some people noticed that regular trash got mixed in with the recycling. I totally get it. The system here is kind of confusing, and it took me a while to figure it out, too. So here's how it works. Plastic, cans, and paper go in the recycling bin, but you need to rinse them first. Food waste goes in a separate bin, and general trash needs a special bag. If you're not sure, just ask me. I can even show you where everything goes. Honestly, it's no big deal, and everyone's happy to help.

When I was a kid, recycling was totally different. We didn't really call it "recycling" back then. We just saved stuff. We had a house with a small yard, so we kept empty bottles in a corner. I would bring old newspapers and bottles to the junk man, and he'd give me a little money or sometimes a few snacks. I got so excited! Plastic wasn't a big deal yet, and most trash just went into one big bag. Now, it's a whole system. We sort plastic, glass, paper, and food waste, and there are rules for everything. It's more work, but I think it's worth it. Looking back, I'd say we're much better at protecting the Earth now.

Well, I have noticed a few changes. The biggest one is that everything is online now. You have to book hotels, trains, and even restaurants on your phone. That's convenient, but if you don't book early, you're out of luck. Last year, I tried to get a room in Gangneung the week before a holiday, and every place was full! The second change is the price. Hotels and food cost a lot more now, so people spend less time traveling. Also, popular places get really crowded. Sometimes you wait an hour just to get a table. So people plan way more now. I'd say travelers are more careful. They compare prices and read reviews, and they travel on weekdays to avoid the crowds.

I'd say the number one concern is money. Travel prices have gone through the roof. That's because more people are traveling, and everything from gas to hotels costs more. The second concern is the crowds. Everyone goes to the same famous spots, thanks to social media. It's like you went on vacation to wait in line! And third, there's safety, like bad weather or accidents. So how do people deal with that? For the money, they use discount apps and look for deals. To avoid the crowds, they go early in the morning or pick a quiet place. And for safety, they buy travel insurance. My friends and I are in the same boat, so we always have a plan B. It helps us relax.
